title: Orogeny of Ethiopian sky islands and Pliocene climate shifts promoted budding speciation and complex admixture in flightless Calosoma ground beetles
content:
Abstract
Flight loss, through its effect on the resulting dispersal capacity and gene flow, has been proposed as a driver of diversification. Ground beetles of the genus Calosoma are unique among the predominantly flightless Carabinae, as nearly half of the species retain flight-capability. Most flightless Calosoma occur in extreme, often isolated habitats such as montane ecosystems. Species in this genus provide an ideal system to investigate the impact of flight loss on diversification across geographical scales. Here, we focus on the flightless species Calosoma (Carabophanus) gestroi, which occurs at high elevations in the southern mountains surrounding the Great Rift Valley of Ethiopia. We investigate genetic differentiation among populations and the biogeographical history of this species across its geographical range using HyRAD-X data. Our results indicate that populations from different mountains form distinct clades, exhibiting both deep genetic differentiation and signatures of recent admixture. The combination of warmer Pliocene climatic conditions and the ongoing orogeny of the Ethiopian highlands promoted an ideal setup for complex cycles of population isolation and admixture. Warm periods drove genetic fixation on either side of the Great Rift Valley, whereas glacial oscillations across emerging sky islands in the Eastern Mountains facilitated genetic homogenization through cycles of allopatric isolation and secondary contact.
